output:
*Interview with Madame Odile Monnier, widow of Aurèle Monnier, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Madame, I am sorry to keep you up, and sorrier for the reason. I will be as brief as I can. Your husband was found in his atelier. You have been told this?

MME MONNIER: I have been told, Inspector. I have not been permitted to see him, and I do not think I shall ask to.

MATTHEY: Let us begin with the household. Who lives in this house?

MME MONNIER: My husband and I. Rosa, who has cooked for us for twelve years. Mademoiselle Ruedi, who works in the atelier. Félix, my husband's nephew, who dined with us tonight. Dr Vauthier is not of the household, but he is of the family, which in this town comes to the same thing.

MATTHEY: How long were you married to Monsieur Monnier?

MME MONNIER: Thirty years. I was a pastor's daughter from Neuchâtel and he was a watchmaker, and he never let me forget that a watch either keeps the time or it does not. I thought that was a clever remark when I was twenty-five. I have had thirty years to change my mind about it.

MATTHEY: Tell me about the evening, as far as you are able.

MME MONNIER: We dined at the usual hour. When the temple bell struck nine, my husband made everyone show their watches, as he has done every year. He tells each owner what is wrong with it. Félix's watch showed twenty minutes to nine. My husband scolded him for it in front of the others. Félix laughed, as he does when he is embarrassed, and said it was his father's watch and nobody was to touch it.

MATTHEY: Was there any disagreement at dinner?

MME MONNIER: There was a quarrel between my husband and Monsieur Girard about the repeater. Monsieur Girard wished to buy the right to it and would not pay what my husband asked. They raised their voices. I did not follow the sums and I will not pretend to.

MATTHEY: And after dinner?

MME MONNIER: We went into the salon. The doctor and I played piquet. He is a poor loser and an unrepentant cheat at cards, and we know each other's faults well after thirty years. We played without a break. The temple struck ten while we played.

MATTHEY: Did the game continue?

MME MONNIER: It did. We played on until he went out to fetch his cigars. I did not look at the clock when he went.

MATTHEY: As he went out, did he say anything to you?

MME MONNIER: He asked me to play for him. I sat down at the piano at once and played until he came back, and I stopped when he came in.

MATTHEY: You play often?

MME MONNIER: I play Chopin, which my husband considered sentimental and listened to anyway. My mother taught me. I was never as good as she believed.

MATTHEY: When he came back, what happened next?

MME MONNIER: A moment after he came back, the hall clock struck eleven.

MATTHEY: Did anything happen after that which you think I should know?

MME MONNIER: Nothing that was not ordinary, Inspector. We went on as we had been.

MATTHEY: Félix owes money, I understand.

MME MONNIER: Everyone in Le Locle knows what Félix owes, and Félix does not, or pretends not to. Some of it is owed to Monsieur Girard. My husband had lent him sums before and had stopped doing so. I expect that was discussed tonight as well, though I was not attending to it.

MATTHEY: Thank you, Madame. Can you say more about your husband's state of mind this evening?

MME MONNIER: My husband was himself, which is to say disagreeable, precise and pleased with his own cleverness. If you are looking for a man who was afraid of something, you will not find him in this house. You will find a man who meant to strike a minute repeater at the turn of the century and was quite certain he would.

MATTHEY: Is there anything else you wish to tell me?

MME MONNIER: My husband is dead, Inspector. I have been married to him for thirty years and I do not propose to weep for you in this room. I will answer what you ask me.
